quote: I know that my Redeemer lives; and at last he will stand.
firstReading: Job, overwhelmed by suffering and by the harshness of those around him, begs for pity rather than further accusation. Yet his lament opens into a remarkable confession of hope: he knows that his Redeemer lives and will finally stand in judgment. Even beyond bodily ruin and death, Job trusts that he will see God. His faith does not deny anguish; it entrusts anguish to the living God.
psalmSummary: The psalmist turns toward the Lord with urgent petition, asking God to hear, show mercy, and answer. The deepest desire is not escape from difficulty but the Lord’s face and abiding presence. Though abandonment may seem near, the psalmist chooses confidence: God will receive the faithful. The closing summons is to wait for the Lord with courage, allowing hope in God to strengthen the heart.
gospelSummary: Jesus sends seventy-two disciples ahead of him into places he intends to visit. Their mission begins in prayer before the Lord of the harvest and proceeds in poverty, peace, and dependence upon hospitality. They are to announce that God’s Kingdom has drawn near, heal the sick, and remain where they are welcomed. Jesus also prepares them for refusal: some towns will reject the messengers and thus reject the One who sent them. The disciples are not commanded to compel belief or defend themselves anxiously; they are to bear clear witness, leave even rejection before God, and continue the mission entrusted to them.
saintReflection: Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus (Memorial): Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus (1873–1897), a Discalced Carmelite and Doctor of the Church, entered the monastery at Lisieux while still young and lived a brief life marked by hidden prayer, obedience, and suffering. Her spiritual teaching, often called the little way, rests on confidence in the Father's mercy and the humble reception of grace. She did not present spiritual childhood as immaturity or passivity; it is the Gospel disposition of one who acknowledges dependence upon God and offers ordinary acts through love. Her desire to serve every vocation in the Church found its center in charity, which gives life to all the members of Christ's Body. Thérèse's witness invites trust when strength is limited, fidelity when holiness is unseen, and missionary prayer rooted in communion with Jesus rather than self-reliance.
dailyPrayer:
Lord Jesus Christ, you send your disciples before you as servants of your peace and heralds of your Kingdom. Grant me the poverty of spirit that receives every good from your hand and does not seek to rely upon myself. When I meet suffering, teach me to bring it before you with Job’s persevering hope: you are my living Redeemer, and you do not abandon those who seek your face.

Through the intercession of Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus, form in me the trustful heart of a spiritual child. Let hidden duties, small acts of patience, and quiet sacrifices become offerings of love united to your sacrifice. Purify me of the desire to be noticed, praised, or successful in the sight of others. Make me faithful in prayer for those who do not know you, for the sick, for those burdened by grief, and for all who labor to proclaim the Gospel.

May your peace dwell in my home and in my words. Give me courage to witness to the nearness of your Kingdom, humility when I am not received, and steadfast hope as I wait for your face. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
The readings reveal a faith that is both afflicted and missionary. Job does not call suffering good, nor does he pretend that accusation and bodily weakness do not wound him. Rather, from within affliction he confesses that his Redeemer lives. Christian hope rests ultimately in the risen Christ, who has entered death and will bring his people into the vision of God. This hope gives suffering a horizon without making suffering itself the final word.

Jesus sends disciples into that same world of vulnerability. They go without worldly security, announcing peace and the approaching Kingdom. Their authority is received, not possessed: they heal and proclaim because Christ sends them. Rejection cannot overturn the truth of the message or remove the disciples from communion with their Lord.

Saint Thérèse illuminates this Gospel mission through her little way. Her hidden Carmel was not a retreat from the Church’s mission, but a place of charity and intercession within Christ’s Body. Spiritual childhood receives grace, perseveres in small acts of love, and trusts the Father amid limitation. In this way, the believer awaits God’s face while making Christ’s peace present.
exegesis:
Context: Job 19:21-27 comes from the depths of Job’s contest with suffering. His companions have treated his affliction as evidence of guilt, multiplying pain instead of offering consolation. Job asks them for mercy because he recognizes that the hand of God has touched him in a mystery he cannot master. He refuses, however, to let their accusations define either God or his own final destiny. The passage moves from an appeal for pity to a confession of astonishing confidence. Job knows that his Redeemer lives. The title evokes one who vindicates and restores the wronged; in the fuller light of Christian faith, this hope is read in relation to Christ, the living Lord who conquers death. Job’s words do not provide a simple explanation for suffering. They witness to fidelity that reaches toward God precisely when visible circumstances seem to contradict hope.

Context: The reading culminates in Job’s certainty that he will see God. This is not a vague consolation or merely a desire that justice should prevail in the present. The language presses beyond bodily decay toward personal encounter with God. The Church hears in it an anticipation of resurrection hope: human life is not discarded by the Creator, and communion with God is stronger than death. Still, Job arrives here through lament. His faith includes pleading, grief, and the cry of one who feels pursued. Such prayer belongs to Scripture because the covenant permits the sufferer to speak truthfully before God. Job teaches that trust is not the suppression of sorrow. It is the persevering refusal to abandon the God whose saving justice remains alive, even when its fulfillment is unseen.

Psalm: Psalm 27 gives prayerful expression to this same movement from distress into confidence. The psalmist asks the Lord to hear, to be gracious, and not to turn away. Beneath these requests lies the central longing of biblical faith: to seek the face of God. God’s face signifies not an abstract idea but the gift of divine presence, favor, and covenant communion. The psalm does not assume that this presence is always emotionally easy to perceive. It speaks to a heart acquainted with fear and apparent abandonment. Yet it answers fear with waiting. Waiting for the Lord is active fidelity: continuing to seek, pray, and hope because God is trustworthy. Courage comes not from self-assurance but from the conviction that the Lord receives those who turn toward him.

Gospel: In Luke 10:1-12, Jesus appoints seventy-two disciples and sends them ahead of him. Their going before the Lord reveals the nature of Christian mission: disciples prepare the way for Christ, rather than drawing attention to themselves. Jesus first commands prayer for laborers, for the harvest belongs to its Lord. Mission therefore begins in adoration and petition, not in human initiative alone. The missionaries are sent as lambs among wolves, a vivid indication that the Gospel’s messengers are not authorized to dominate or retaliate. Their vulnerability corresponds to the Crucified One whom they serve. They travel without possessions meant to secure them, receiving hospitality and daily sustenance as gifts. This dependence makes visible that the Kingdom is God’s work and that its heralds live by the Father’s providence.

Gospel: The disciples’ first word in a house is peace. This peace is more than polite goodwill; it is the blessing associated with God’s reign, offered through those sent by Jesus. Where it is received, the disciples remain, share what is given, and minister to the sick. Their healing and proclamation belong together: the nearness of the Kingdom touches persons in their concrete wounds and summons them to recognize God’s visitation. Jesus also prepares his disciples for rejection. They are to depart without coercion, making clear that the Kingdom has nevertheless come near. Even the dust shaken from their feet is testimony, not vengeance. The warning concerning rejected towns emphasizes the grave responsibility of encountering Christ’s messengers. Yet the disciples are freed from the burden of forcing a response; their task is faithful witness, while judgment belongs to God.

Saints: Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus shows how these readings bear fruit in a life whose outward circumstances were hidden. As a Discalced Carmelite and Doctor of the Church, she received ordinary duties, obedience, illness, and suffering as places where grace could be welcomed and love offered. Her little way is not a diminished Gospel or a refusal of costly discipleship. It is spiritual childhood: the humble acknowledgment that all holiness comes from the Father’s mercy. In this, she stands close to Job’s confession, for both refuse to ground hope in natural strength. Thérèse also shares the missionary heart of Luke’s Gospel. Her desire to serve every vocation found its center in charity, the life of Christ’s Body. Her prayer and hidden love were thus genuinely missionary, united to Jesus who sends laborers into his harvest.

Today: The Church receives these texts as a summons to hope, prayer, and peaceful witness. When suffering brings questions that cannot quickly be answered, Job directs believers toward the living Redeemer and the promised vision of God. When fear tempts the heart to imagine abandonment, the psalm calls it again to seek the Lord’s face and wait with courage. When the Church announces the Gospel, Luke insists that her manner must resemble Jesus: prayerful, poor in spirit, peace-bearing, attentive to the sick, and free from coercion. Saint Thérèse teaches that this mission is not confined to visible works. A hidden act performed through love, a patient acceptance of limitation, and persevering intercession can participate in Christ’s saving mission. The Kingdom is near because Christ is near; his disciples bear that nearness by receiving grace, loving faithfully, and entrusting every outcome to him.
